question: Air density is defined as:

options.text: Pressure per unit temperature
Weight per unit area
Mass per unit volume
Volume per unit mass

explanation: Density is mass per unit volume, for example grams per cubic metre. ISA sea-level density is 1225 g/m³.

question: Relative density expresses the density of a sample of air as:

options.text: A percentage of the ISA sea-level density
A percentage of the density of water
The altitude in the ISA at which that density occurs
The ratio of its pressure to its temperature

explanation: Relative density compares actual density with the standard surface value of 1225 g/m³, so 74% means 74% of ISA sea-level density.

question: Density altitude is:

options.text: The height above the aerodrome at which the air density is half its surface value
The altitude shown on the altimeter with 1013 hPa set
True altitude corrected for temperature
The altitude in the standard atmosphere at which the observed density would occur

explanation: Density altitude is a way of stating density as a height: it is the ISA altitude that has the same density as the air being considered. A high density altitude means thin air and poorer performance.

subtopic: Effects of pressure, temperature and humidity
question: If the temperature is constant, an increase in pressure will:

options.text: Leave density unchanged
Increase density, since density is directly proportional to pressure
Decrease density, since density is inversely proportional to pressure
Increase density only if humidity also increases

explanation: Compressing air reduces its volume for the same mass, so density rises in proportion to pressure (ρ = P/RT).

subtopic: Effects of pressure, temperature and humidity
question: If the pressure is constant, an increase in temperature will:

options.text: Decrease density, since density is inversely proportional to absolute temperature
Leave density unchanged, since only pressure affects density
Increase density, since warm air holds more molecules in each cubic metre of volume
Increase density, but only in moist air near saturation

explanation: Heated air expands, so the same mass occupies more volume and density falls.

subtopic: Effects of pressure, temperature and humidity
question: At constant pressure and temperature, adding water vapour to a sample of air will:

options.text: Leave its density unchanged, because the pressure stays the same
Increase its density, because liquid water is much heavier than air
Decrease its density, since water molecules are lighter than N₂ and O₂
Increase its density, but only once the air is close to saturation

explanation: The molecular mass of water (about 18) is lower than that of nitrogen (28) or oxygen (32). Replacing them with water molecules reduces the mass in a given volume, so moist air is less dense than dry air.

subtopic: Effects of pressure, temperature and humidity
question: As a rule of thumb, density changes by about 1% for a change of:

options.text: 1°C in temperature or 1 hPa in pressure
3°C in temperature or 10 hPa in pressure
30°C in temperature or 100 hPa in pressure
10°C in temperature or 30 hPa in pressure

explanation: Near the surface absolute temperature is about 288 K and pressure about 1013 hPa, so 1% of each is roughly 3°C and 10 hPa.

subtopic: Effects of pressure, temperature and humidity
question: Which combination produces the lowest air density at an aerodrome?

options.text: Low elevation, high temperature and low humidity
Low elevation, low temperature and low humidity
High elevation, low temperature and low humidity
High elevation, high temperature and high humidity

explanation: Low pressure (high elevation), high temperature and high water-vapour content all reduce density. "High, hot and humid" is the worst case for performance.

subtopic: Effects of pressure, temperature and humidity
question: Compared with its effect on density, the effect of humidity is normally:

options.text: Always negligible, so it is never taken into account in performance
Small, but worth allowing for at hot, very humid aerodromes
Larger than the effect of temperature, at all aerodromes
Larger than the effect of pressure, especially at high elevations

explanation: Humidity has only a small effect on density, but where the air is both very warm and very moist it becomes significant for take-off performance.

question: Density decreases with height in the troposphere because:

options.text: Temperature increases with height, which expands the air
Pressure and temperature both increase with height above the friction layer
The fall in pressure has a much greater effect than the fall in temperature
Humidity increases with height, and moist air is less dense

explanation: Falling temperature on its own would increase density, but pressure falls proportionally much faster, so overall density decreases with height.

question: In the ISA, density is roughly 50% of its sea-level value at:

options.text: About 20 000 ft
About 5000 ft
About 40 000 ft
About 10 000 ft

explanation: As an approximation, ISA density is about 50% at 20 000 ft, 25% at 40 000 ft and 10% at 60 000 ft.

question: In the ISA, density at 40 000 ft is roughly:

options.text: 10% of the sea-level value
75% of the sea-level value
50% of the sea-level value
25% of the sea-level value

explanation: Density roughly halves again between 20 000 ft (about 50%) and 40 000 ft (about 25%).

question: At the surface, moving from the Equator towards the poles, air density generally:

options.text: Increases, because the air is colder
Stays the same, because MSL pressure is the same
Decreases, because the air is colder
Increases only in summer

explanation: Surface pressures are broadly similar, but polar air is much colder, so surface density increases with latitude.

question: At about which level is air density roughly the same at all latitudes?

options.text: About 10 000 ft
At the surface
About 50 000 ft
About 26 000 ft

explanation: Near the surface cold polar air is densest; high up the relationship reverses. The crossover where density hardly changes with latitude is around 26 000 ft.

question: At about 50 000 ft, density over the poles compared with density over the Equator is:

options.text: The same, because density is constant at all latitudes at 50 000 ft
Higher, because the air over the poles is colder at all levels
Lower, because pressure falls off more quickly with height in cold air
Higher in summer and lower in winter, with no average difference

explanation: Pressure falls more slowly with height in warm equatorial air, so at high levels pressure is much higher over the Equator. That outweighs the colder temperature there, so high-level density is greater over the Equator and lower over the poles.

question: The greatest departure of density from the ISA value because of latitude occurs at about:

options.text: The surface

explanation: The latitude effect on density reverses at about 26 000 ft and is largest, in the opposite sense to the surface effect, at about 50 000 ft.

question: In the lift equation L = CL ½ρV²S, a reduction in air density at a given TAS will:

options.text: Reduce lift, so a higher TAS is needed to lift the same weight
Increase lift, because the reduced drag allows a higher speed
Reduce lift, but only above the tropopause where the air is thin
Have no effect on lift, because lift depends only on IAS and angle of attack

explanation: Lift is directly proportional to density. Thin air needs a higher true airspeed for the same lift, so take-off and landing runs are longer.

question: Low air density at an aerodrome will:

options.text: Reduce the TAS needed for take-off
Reduce the take-off run and increase the maximum take-off mass
Increase the take-off run and reduce the maximum take-off mass
Increase engine power output

explanation: Low density reduces both lift and engine thrust or power, so more runway is needed and the permissible take-off mass may have to be reduced.

question: Which group of aerodromes is most likely to have performance limited by low density because of high elevation?

options.text: Anchorage, Reykjavik and Oslo
Denver, Nairobi and Sana'a
Bahrain, Khartoum and Singapore
Amsterdam, London and Copenhagen

explanation: Denver, Nairobi and Sana'a lie at high elevations, so pressure, and therefore density, is low. Bahrain, Khartoum and Singapore are low but hot, and in some cases humid.

question: Singapore and Bahrain are low-lying, yet take-off performance can suffer there mainly because of:

options.text: High aerodrome elevation above mean sea level
Very low temperatures and dense, dry air
Frequent strong winds and associated turbulence
High temperatures together with high humidity

explanation: These aerodromes are near sea level, so pressure is normal, but high temperature and high moisture content both reduce density.

question: Air density affects the accuracy of:

options.text: The clock and the fuel quantity gauges, through temperature changes
Radio altimeters only, through changes in signal propagation
The magnetic compass only, through changes in air conductivity
Airspeed and Mach indications, and aircraft and engine performance

explanation: Pressure instruments such as the ASI respond to dynamic pressure, which depends on density. Density also governs lift, drag and engine output.

question: An aircraft takes off at a high aerodrome on a hot day. Compared with a sea-level ISA day at the same IAS, its TAS will be:

options.text: The same, because IAS is the same
Higher, because the air is less dense
Higher only if the humidity is low
Lower, because the air is less dense

explanation: For the same dynamic pressure (IAS), lower density requires a higher true airspeed. The ground run therefore lengthens even though the indicated rotation speed is unchanged.

question: In which situation will density altitude be higher than the aerodrome elevation?

options.text: Only when the aerodrome is below MSL
Whenever QNH is above 1013 hPa
When the temperature is above ISA for that elevation
When the temperature is below ISA for that elevation

explanation: Warmer-than-standard air is less dense, so it corresponds to the density of a higher ISA altitude. Low pressure has the same effect.

question: On a cold winter day with high pressure, air density at a sea-level aerodrome will be:

options.text: Higher than ISA, so performance is better than standard
Lower than ISA, so performance is worse than standard
Exactly the ISA value
Lower than ISA, because cold air holds less water

explanation: Low temperature and high pressure both increase density. The density altitude is then below the aerodrome elevation.

question: Two aerodromes have the same elevation and the same QNH. Aerodrome A is at +35°C, aerodrome B at +5°C. Which is true?

options.text: A has the lower density altitude because warm air rises
A has the higher density altitude and the poorer take-off performance
Both have the same density altitude because their pressures are equal
B has the higher density altitude and the poorer take-off performance

explanation: At equal pressure, the warmer air is less dense, so A's density altitude is higher and its performance worse.

question: Air at a given level is described as having a relative density of 60%. This means:

options.text: It is 60% saturated with respect to water vapour
Its pressure is 60% of the standard 1013 hPa
Its density is 60% of the ISA sea-level density
Its relative humidity is 60%, measured by psychrometer

explanation: Relative density compares density with the standard sea-level value, not with humidity or pressure.

question: In a column of warm air, compared with a column of cold air with the same surface pressure, the density at 10 000 ft will be:

options.text: Exactly the same, because both columns have the same surface pressure
Much higher, because pressure aloft is so much higher in the warm column
Higher, because the warm column contains more water vapour at all levels
Somewhat lower, because at this level the warm column is still less dense

explanation: At low levels the temperature effect dominates: warm air is less dense. Only well up in the troposphere (around 26 000 ft and above) does the higher pressure in the warm column reverse the comparison.

question: Air density at an aerodrome is reduced by 3% by a rise in temperature alone. The temperature rise was about:
explanation: About 1% per 3°C, so 3% corresponds to about 9°C.

question: A fall of 20 hPa in pressure at constant temperature would change density by about:
explanation: About 1% per 10 hPa, so 20 hPa gives about 2%, and lower pressure means lower density.

question: Which of the following increases air density?

options.text: A fall in temperature at constant pressure
An increase in water vapour content
A rise in temperature at constant pressure
A decrease in pressure at constant temperature

explanation: Colder air at the same pressure is denser.
